With world-renowned cultural campuses, San Diego is one of the country’s top 100 arts communities, but can San Diego hold its position amid shrinking arts investment and rising costs?

San Diego’s art scene is one of most vibrant in the country, but San Diego’s art scene luster is dimming, as public funding dries up and artists’ pay falls behind the curve amid soaring housing costs and inflation.

The San Diego region is among the top 10 percent nationwide, based on the number of artists and cultural organizations, total dollars spent on the arts, and government funding, according to an analysis of community arts vibrancy by Southern Methodist University in Texas.

The region boasts cultural campuses such as Balboa Park, the Jacobs Music Center, and California Center for the Arts, Escondido. Plus, scores of galleries, performance spaces and concert venues add up to a robust art scene.

Illinois and Maryland ranked just above California.

“Not surprisingly, there’s strong correlations between the wealth of a community and the arts vibrancy rankings,” Jen Benoit-Bryan said.

Researchers group areas into clusters of peer cities: areas of similar size, demographic characteristics and rankings. San Diego is grouped with Denver, Atlanta, Miami and Houston, Denver, Atlanta, Miami and Houston fall in the 87th to 94th percentiles for arts vibrancy, according to the study.

percentiles for arts vibrancy, according to the study.

Of Denver, Atlanta, Miami and Houston, only Atlanta improved its status in recent years. Denver, Atlanta, Miami and Houston, including San Diego, declined.

Near the top, but slipping

San Diego’s for-profit arts sector remains strong, Jen Benoit-Bryan said. But public investment in the arts is waning.

said. But public investment in the arts is waning.

The number of arts and culture organizations per capita across San Diego and its peer cities is consistently declining, Jen Benoit-Bryan said. In San Diego, the number of employees in the cultural workforce is also falling. That’s possibly because employees in the cultural workforce can’t afford to keep employees in the cultural workforce jobs.

to keep employees in the cultural workforce jobs.

“We see that the compensation levels for the kind of workers in non-profit cultural organizations are also lower than peers and have been declining over the last few years,” Jen Benoit-Bryan said. “And federal dollars that are flowing into cultural organizations in San Diego are again lower than peers and in decline.”

Diego are again lower than peers and in decline.”

The University of San Diego study found similar results. Nonprofits of all types are facing financial pressure, Tess Tinkler said, with 80% of nonprofit leaders reporting a drop in funding from  government foundations, individual donors and corporate sponsors, said Tess Tinkler, director of research for University of San Diego Nonprofit Institute.

arts organizations is worse than other nonprofits.”

Adjusting for inflation, arts employees’ wages have not grown over the past 13 years, and have actually dropped in real dollars since 2012, Tinkler said. Meanwhile, arts employees face rising costs for necessities such as gas and housing; San Diego consistently ranks as one of the most expensive home markets in the country.

Healthcare costs are another sticking point for arts employers, said Jessica Hanson York, executive director of the Mingei International Museum in Balboa Park

“Jessica Hanson York are still able to cover the cost of healthcare for Mingei International Museum employees, but Jessica Hanson York are stretched to the maximum to keep up,” Jessica Hanson York said.

How to turn the tide?

Arts and culture programs might seem to fall into the nice-to-have spending category, but arts advocates say arts and culture programs’re bellwethers for community well-being.

programs’re bellwethers for community well-being.

The University of San Diego report cited research showing that involvement with the arts increases social connection, reduces anxiety and depression, and helps with youth development and academic accomplishment.

with community health providers “as appropriate.”

amendments also broadened what colleges would report to the state, allowing community colleges to count medication abortion provided through outside healthcare providers instead of only those performed at community college health centers.

Assembly Bill 2540 was referred to the Senate Health and Education committees on June 10. After amendments, Assembly Bill 2540 was re-referred July 2 to the Senate Appropriations Committee, where lawmakers will review its fiscal impact.

already required at the state’s public universities.

Assembly Bill 2540 would require community colleges with student health centers to offer access to medication abortion beginning in 2029, if the Legislature provides funding. Assembly Bill 2540 builds on Senate Bill 24, Senate Bill 24 that requires University of California and California State University student health centers to provide medication abortion beginning in 2023.

Assembly Bill 2540 would require community colleges with health centers to provide access to medication abortion if lawmakers provide funding. health center directors say community colleges lack the staffing and infrastructure to offer the service.

community college students could gain access to medication abortion through community college health centers under Assembly Bill 2540 that would extend reproductive health services already required at the state’s public universities.

college health centers vary in size and services

But while supporters frame Assembly Bill 2540 as a matter of equal access, health center directors say implementing Assembly Bill 2540 statewide may be far more complicated than applying University of California and California State University student health centers.

services out to community providers and hospitals.”

Health Services Association of California Community Colleges, which represents student health programs across the system, opposes Assembly Bill 2540. In an April 15 letter to lawmakers, Health Services Association of California Community Colleges said community college health centers do not prescribe medication, nor do community college health centers have sufficient staffing or the infrastructure needed to provide medication abortion onsite.

to provide medication abortion beginning in 2023.

supporters say Assembly Bill 2540 would close an access gap for community college students who may face transportation, cost, privacy or insurance barriers when medication abortion is only available off campus. But health center directors warn that community colleges may not have the funding, staffing or clinical capacity to provide medication abortion.
